From a published key to a field key

Source: vignettes/published-key.Rmd
published-key.Rmd

Most keys already exist: as text in a flora, a revision or a field guide. This vignette takes one from the printed page to a phone in five steps: read the text, check it, cut it down to the place you work in, see how quickly it reaches a result, and export it as a page that opens without signal.

The steps that ask a web service (GBIF) are shown with the output of a run on 19 November 2026 and are not run when the vignette is built. Everything else runs as written.

library(dimoose)

1. Read the text

The example is a short key to the broadleaf trees of a river bottom, written for dimoose in the layout of a regional flora: numbered couplets with a and b leads, dot leaders, wrapped lines, authorities, common names and page references.

file <- system.file("extdata", "textkeys", "trees-bracketed.txt", package = "dimoose")
writeLines(readLines(file)[1:11])
#> Key to the Broadleaf Trees of the Cottonwood Bottoms
#> 
#> 1a. Leaves opposite on the twig ........................................ 2
#> 1b. Leaves alternate on the twig ....................................... 4
#> 2a. Leaves simple, palmately lobed, the lobes sharply
#>     toothed ................... Acer glabrum Torr. (Rocky Mountain maple)
#> 2b. Leaves pinnately compound .......................................... 3
#> 3a. Leaflets 3 to 5, coarsely toothed or shallowly lobed; fruit a
#>     paired samara ........................... Acer negundo L. (boxelder)
#> 3b. Leaflets 5 to 9, finely toothed; fruit a single pad-
#>     dle-shaped samara ........... Fraxinus pennsylvanica Marshall, p. 118

keyFromText() takes a file, one string or a vector of lines:

trees <- keyFromText(file)
trees
#> <dimoose key> Key to the Broadleaf Trees of the Cottonwood Bottoms
#>   8 couplets, 16 leads, 9 taxa, up to 5 steps deep (3.6 on average)
trees$leads[1:6, c("Statement", "Choice", "Character", "Next", "Taxon", "CommonName")]
#>   Statement Choice                                                                   Character Next
#> 1         1      a                                                 Leaves opposite on the twig    2
#> 2         1      b                                                Leaves alternate on the twig    4
#> 3         2      a                   Leaves simple, palmately lobed, the lobes sharply toothed    -
#> 4         2      b                                                   Leaves pinnately compound    3
#> 5         3      a Leaflets 3 to 5, coarsely toothed or shallowly lobed; fruit a paired samara    -
#> 6         3      b        Leaflets 5 to 9, finely toothed; fruit a single paddle-shaped samara    -
#>                    Taxon           CommonName
#> 1                                            
#> 2                                            
#> 3           Acer glabrum Rocky Mountain maple
#> 4                                            
#> 5           Acer negundo             boxelder
#> 6 Fraxinus pennsylvanica

Each lead’s destination is a couplet number or a taxon. The authority, the common name and the page are split off into columns of their own, so Taxon holds the bare name. It also reads leads marked 1./1'., A./AA., a number and a dash, back-references such as 3(1)., and indented keys. Indented keys whose leads have no number or letter at all are not handled.

2. Check it

keyFromText() checks what it built and keeps a report with the key. Here the only entry is a note: a word hyphenated at a line end was joined.

trees$validate()          # no structural problems
attr(trees, "problems")
#>   Line Couplet Lead Kind         Type                                   Message
#> 1   10       3   3b note dehyphenated joined 1 word(s) hyphenated at a line end

Scanned text is rougher. parseTextKey() gives the lead table and the report without building the key, which is the place to start with a scan. This one has a l where a 1 should be and a lead that lost its dot leaders:

scan <- system.file("extdata", "textkeys", "meadow-ocr.txt", package = "dimoose")
parseTextKey(scan)
#> <parsed text key> 8 leads in 4 couplets, bracketed layout
#>   Key to the Grasslike Plants of the Wet Meadow
#>   0 problem(s), 2 repair(s), 3 note(s)
#>   line 3: read the label 'l.' as couplet 1 [repaired]
#>   line 15: no dot leaders before the destination; took the trailing 'Scirpus microcarpus' as the taxon [repaired]

Repairs are reported, never silent, and strict = TRUE stops instead of repairing. A lead with no destination, a couplet with one lead or a missing couplet is a problem, reported with its line; no lead is dropped. These checks were written against keys made for the purpose; expect to correct a few lines by hand on a real scan.

A printed key’s names may be out of date. checkNames() looks them up in the GBIF backbone taxonomy:

checkNames(trees, kingdom = "Plantae")[, c("Taxon", "status", "accepted")]
#>                                    Taxon  status               accepted
#> 1                           Acer glabrum      ok           Acer glabrum
#> 2                           Acer negundo      ok           Acer negundo
#> 3                 Fraxinus pennsylvanica      ok Fraxinus pennsylvanica
#> 4                                  Salix      ok                  Salix
#> 5                      Betula papyrifera      ok      Betula papyrifera
#> 6                    Betula occidentalis      ok    Betula occidentalis
#> 7                    Populus tremuloides      ok    Populus tremuloides
#> 8                   Populus angustifolia      ok   Populus angustifolia
#> 9 Populus balsamifera subsp. trichocarpa synonym    Populus trichocarpa

3. Cut it down to a place

A regional flora covers more than any one county. regionalKey() asks GBIF which of the key’s taxa have been recorded in a place, drops the others, and closes up the couplets that no longer split anything. Here the place is Flathead County, Montana, by its GADM id, and a taxon needs five records to stay:

local <- regionalKey(trees, "USA.27.15_1", kingdom = "Plantae", minRecords = 5, renumber = TRUE)
#> Kept 8 of 9 taxa recorded in GADM region USA.27.15_1 (GBIF)
attr(local, "records")[, c("Taxon", "records", "kept")]
#>                                    Taxon records  kept
#> 1                           Acer glabrum     272  TRUE
#> 2                           Acer negundo      11  TRUE
#> 3                 Fraxinus pennsylvanica       1 FALSE
#> 4                                  Salix     348  TRUE
#> 5                      Betula papyrifera      70  TRUE
#> 6                    Betula occidentalis      13  TRUE
#> 7                    Populus tremuloides      93  TRUE
#> 8                   Populus angustifolia       7  TRUE
#> 9 Populus balsamifera subsp. trichocarpa      56  TRUE

The table is the audit trail: every taxon, the number of records and whether it was kept. A place can also be a name ("Flathead County, Montana"), a two-letter country code or a polygon, and source = "inat" counts iNaturalist research-grade observations instead. With the default minRecords = 1 all nine taxa of this key stay. Record counts say where people have looked as much as what grows there, so read the table before trusting the cut.

pruneKey() makes the same cut from a list of names, with no web service. So that the rest of this vignette runs offline, it is used here to drop the one taxon GBIF dropped above:

local <- pruneKey(trees, drop = "Fraxinus pennsylvanica", renumber = TRUE)
local
#> <dimoose key> Key to the Broadleaf Trees of the Cottonwood Bottoms
#>   7 couplets, 14 leads, 8 taxa, up to 5 steps deep (3.5 on average)
local$validate()
local$leads[1:4, c("Statement", "Character", "Next", "Taxon", "Note")]
#>   Statement                                                 Character Next        Taxon
#> 1         1                               Leaves opposite on the twig    2             
#> 2         1                              Leaves alternate on the twig    3             
#> 3         2 Leaves simple, palmately lobed, the lobes sharply toothed    - Acer glabrum
#> 4         2                                 Leaves pinnately compound    - Acer negundo
#>                                                                          Note
#> 1                                                                            
#> 2                                                                            
#> 3                                                                            
#> 4 Leaflets 3 to 5, coarsely toothed or shallowly lobed; fruit a paired samara

Couplet 3 of the original told box elder from green ash. With green ash gone it no longer splits anything, so it was removed and its lead now ends at box elder directly. What it said about box elder is kept in the Note column, as a character to confirm the result with. mergeKeys() goes the other way and grafts a second key onto a result, for example a key to the willows onto Salix.

4. How quickly does it reach a result? 

summary(local)[c("couplets", "taxa", "depth", "meanTaxonSteps", "bound", "efficiency")]
#>   couplets taxa depth meanTaxonSteps bound efficiency
#> 1        7    8     5            3.5     3  0.8571429

meanTaxonSteps is the number of couplets a reader answers, on average over the eight taxa. bound is what the best possible key to the same taxa would need: eight equally common taxa cannot be told apart in fewer than three two-way steps. efficiency is the bound over the steps taken.

The taxa are not equally likely, though. Weighted by the record counts above (which occurrenceWeights(local, region = "USA.27.15_1", kingdom = "Plantae") fetches in one call), the key does better than its plain average, because the two commonest taxa key out in two steps:

w <- c("Acer glabrum" = 272, "Acer negundo" = 11, "Salix" = 348, "Betula papyrifera" = 70,
       "Betula occidentalis" = 13, "Populus tremuloides" = 93, "Populus angustifolia" = 7,
       "Populus balsamifera subsp. trichocarpa" = 56)
summary(local, weights = w)[c("meanTaxonSteps", "expectedSteps", "bound", "efficiency")]
#>   meanTaxonSteps expectedSteps    bound efficiency
#> 1            3.5      2.621839 2.224138  0.8483121
q <- keyQuality(local, weights = w)$taxa
q[order(-q$weight), c("Taxon", "steps", "weight")]
#>                                    Taxon steps      weight
#> 3                                  Salix     2 0.400000000
#> 1                           Acer glabrum     2 0.312643678
#> 6                    Populus tremuloides     4 0.106896552
#> 4                      Betula papyrifera     4 0.080459770
#> 8 Populus balsamifera subsp. trichocarpa     5 0.064367816
#> 5                    Betula occidentalis     4 0.014942529
#> 2                           Acer negundo     2 0.012643678
#> 7                   Populus angustifolia     5 0.008045977

Real keys rarely reach an efficiency of 1, because the characters that would split the taxa evenly may not exist. Use it to compare keys to the same taxa, not as a mark out of one.

5. Take it into the field 

site <- file.path(tempdir(), "site")
dir.create(site, showWarnings = FALSE)
page <- exportWizard(local, file.path(site, "flathead-trees.html"), offline = TRUE)
list.files(site)
#> [1] "flathead-trees-icon-192.png" "flathead-trees-icon-512.png" "flathead-trees-sw.js"       
#> [4] "flathead-trees.html"         "flathead-trees.webmanifest"

flathead-trees.html is the whole key in one file: it asks one couplet at a time, has an “I’m not sure” choice that follows both leads, a map of the key, and Back. offline = TRUE adds a web app manifest, a service worker and two icons. Put all five files in one folder of an https website, open the page once on the phone while it has a connection, and add it to the home screen; after that it opens without signal. A page opened straight from disk works too, but is not installed. The offline part has been tested with a simulated browser and not yet on a phone, so try it before you rely on it.

To correct a lead or add photos, write the key out as the spreadsheet keyFromSpreadsheet() reads, edit it, and read it back (see vignette("montana-hardwoods")):

csv <- keyToSpreadsheet(local, file.path(site, "flathead-trees.csv"))
#> Not written to the spreadsheet: the leads' Authority, CommonName, Page, Line columns
back <- keyFromSpreadsheet(csv, desc = "Trees of Flathead County")
back
#> <dimoose key> Trees of Flathead County
#>   7 couplets, 14 leads, 8 taxa, up to 5 steps deep (3.5 on average)

The spreadsheet keeps the leads and their photos; the title and the extra columns (Note, Authority, CommonName, Page) are not written.
